lead: Lakewood grew up fast in the 1950s to 1970s, and many of those ranch homes still have original pipes. Hail, freeze-thaw swings and basement leaks keep it busy.
risk: aging pipes, hail damage and basement leaks
why: The median Lakewood home was built in 1977, and many neighborhoods are full of brick ranches and split-levels from the decades before that. Those homes often still have galvanized steel supply lines, which rust from the inside and start to leak. Many also have basements. A failed water heater, a cracked pipe or a backed-up floor drain can soak carpet and drywall down there fast.

Lakewood sits right against the foothills on the west side of the Denver metro, in one of the busiest hail zones in the country. Spring and summer storms crack shingles and dent gutters, and leaks show up in the next rain. Winter brings fast temperature swings. A warm chinook day followed by a hard freeze can split pipes in outside walls and garages.
image_alt: Hailstones scattered on wet wood after a storm
image_caption: Hail and fast storms off the foothills leave Lakewood roofs open to leaks.
problems: 1950s to 1970s homes in Eiber, Morse Park
tips: Have a plumber check for old galvanized pipe.
Get the roof inspected after any hail, even with no leak yet.
Disconnect garden hoses before the first freeze.
Test the sump pump and floor drain each spring.
areas: Calls come from Belmar, Green Mountain, Bear Creek, Union Square, Two Creeks, Eiber, Morse Park and Lasley, plus Wheat Ridge, Golden and Littleton.

faq.q: How do I know if my Lakewood home has galvanized pipes?
faq.a: Look at the pipe where it enters the house or near the water heater. Galvanized pipe is dull gray and threaded at the joints. A magnet will stick to it, but not to copper. Low water pressure and rusty water are common signs. Replacing it now costs far less than drying out a flooded basement.
